Benchmarking against reference assemblies demonstrates that ImpuT2T is highly effective at patching human HiFi assemblies, consistently outperforming existing patching approaches. Moreover, we show that including more haplotypes in the pangenome improves the quality of the patched assemblies, with the greatest gains achieved using the full HPRC Release 2 pangenome.

items.title: A dCas9 Proximity Reporter for Investigating DNA Linear and Rotational Dynamics
items.blurb: The dCas9 system has rapidly been developed into many tools to explore different aspects of the human genome; the high binding specificity, coupled with the inactive nuclease enzyme, allows for precise recruitment of molecules to specific sequences of DNA. We sought to exploit these capabilities to create a tool for assessing the real-time proximity of two DNA sequences within a biological system. By incorporating aptamers into gRNAs, dCas9 molecules can be used to recruit the {beta}9 or {beta}10 strands of split-NanoLuc(R) to specific DNA sequences and quantify the proximity of those sequences based on their ability to complex with the luciferase fragment ({Delta}11S) and produce luminescence. While many tools exist to detect a single DNA sequence, this system is uniquely capable of assessing how two DNA sequences interact with each other. As expected, we found that the interaction of two dCas9 molecules was affected by their linear distance from each other on dsDNA. Surprisingly, we found that their interaction was also strongly influenced by rotational orientation, even for sequences that are close together in linear space. This finding indicates that dCas9 rotational alignment is an important consideration for designing dCas9 systems that target multiple DNA sequences simultaneously. Beyond the findings presented herein, we believe this DNA proximity detection tool has the potential to be adapted for applications involving the proximity and orientation of two DNA sequences.

items.title: Transplanting enzyme active site geometry into antibody CDRs for catalytic antibody design
items.blurb: Antibodies provide programmable molecular recognition, whereas enzymes enable repeated chemical transformation. Catalytic antibodies seek to combine these properties within a single protein scaffold. However, conventional approaches based on transition state analogue immunisation, library screening or local mutagenesis provide limited control over the atomic arrangement of catalytic residues. They also frequently produce antibodies that bind substrates without supporting efficient chemical turnover. Recent advances in generative protein design have enabled the construction of antibody complementarity determining regions and the scaffolding of functional motifs under structural constraints. A systematic strategy for transferring experimentally supported enzyme active site geometry into antibody variable domains is still lacking. Here, we present a computational framework that treats antibody and enzyme structures as distinct but complementary inputs. Developable Fv or VHH structures provide the immunoglobulin scaffold. Enzyme complexes containing substrates, products or transition state analogues provide catalytic residues, ligand conformations, metals, cofactors and key water networks. The selected catalytic atoms are mapped into antibody complementarity determining regions, while the surrounding loops are reconstructed using antibody compatible representations and constrained all atom diffusion. Sequence design and structural back prediction are followed by filters for antibody folding, catalytic geometry, ligand positioning, conformational stability and developability. The framework avoids direct fusion of intact enzymes and antibodies. Instead, it transfers only the local geometry required for catalysis. This separation of scaffold selection from catalytic motif selection creates a testable route for determining whether natural enzyme chemistry can be embedded within antibody formats. It also provides a practical basis for evaluating substrate binding, chemical conversion, product release and catalytic turnover as separate design objectives.

items.title: Sequence determinants of pathogenicity in glucose-6-phosphatase linked to glycogen storage disease type 1a
items.blurb: Glycogen storage disease type 1a (GSD1a) is an autosomal recessive Mendelian disorder that can be caused by missense variants in glucose-6-phosphatase catalytic subunit 1 (G6PC1). Although hundreds of missense variants have been identified, the vast majority are of unknown clinical significance, and the molecular mechanism(s) of bona fide pathogenic variants are ill-defined. We combine bioinformatic data and clinical associations with the protein language model AlphaMissense to guide mechanistic exploration of 78 missense variants at 55 residue positions using robust biochemical and biophysical assays to distill general principles of enzyme dysfunction. Correlation analysis established a strong linear relationship between folded G6PC1 abundance and catalytic capacity for most variants. Pathogenic variants within this paradigm were linked to compromised stability and activation of the unfolded protein response. However, outliers characterized by relatively high abundance, yet low activity clustered to a network of sidechains adjacent to the active site that allosterically modulate catalysis. Contextualized by recent high-resolution structures and AlphaFold modeling, our holistic analysis of G6PC1 in vitro metrics facilitates clinical (re)classification of variants according to explicit molecular phenotypes and identifies therapeutic design directions. Moreover, our approach illustrates a blueprint for variant characterization that integrates computational prediction with experimental validation to discover disease etiology.

items.title: Transcriptomic datasets of melittin- and un-treated murine cervical carcinoma U14 cells
items.blurb: Melittin, a potent amphipathic cationic peptide derived from bee venom, exhibits broad-spectrum antineoplastic efficacy, notably against cervical carcinoma. Despite its established therapeutic potential, the global transcriptional reprogramming orchestrating its acute multi-pathway cytotoxicity remains incompletely understood. To bridge this knowledge gap, we generated the first comprehensive, untargeted RNA-seq dataset profiling the acute phase of melittin-induced cell death in murine cervical carcinoma U14 cells (exposed to 4 g/mL melittin for 20 minutes) alongside untreated controls. Utilizing deep sequencing and rigorous bioinformatics workflows, we quantified genome-wide mRNA abundances and mapped a distinct transcriptomic shift, identifying 254 significantly differentially expressed genes (DEGs), comprising 158 up- and 96 down-regulated transcripts. Validated by stringent quality control metrics, exceptional genomic mapping rates, and comprehensive functional annotations via the GO and KEGG databases, this high-resolution transcriptomic resource provides a systems-level map of early molecular alterations. All raw and processed sequencing data are publicly available. This transcriptomic resource provides a valuable foundation for elucidating the acute regulatory networks underlying melittin-induced anti-cervical cancer effects.

items.title: Pangenome Analysis Reveals Gene Content Variation and Evolutionary Dynamics Across the Culex pipiens Species Complex
items.blurb: The Culex pipiens species complex contains the principal northern-hemisphere vectors of West Nile virus, lymphatic filariasis and several arboviruses; yet, the genomic basis of its diversity remains poorly resolved. We present the first pangenome characterization of the four widely recognized Cx. pipiens complex forms (Cx. pipiens, Cx. pallens, Cx. quinquefasciatus, Cx. molestus), with Cx. tarsalis as outgroup. From chromosome-scale assemblies (533-790 Mb) and unified annotations transferred from the Cx. quinquefasciatus reference, we identified 16,568 orthogroups. Restricted to the ingroup, 92,821 genes (98.2%) were partitioned into 11,284 core (71.1%), 3,726 shell (23.5%) and 871 cloud (5.5%) orthogroups. Form-specific cloud orthogroups were unevenly distributed (chi-squared = 71.9, p = 1.7e-15), with Cx. molestus carrying the largest set. A concatenated 8,067-locus phylogeny placed Cx. pallens and Cx. quinquefasciatus as sisters with full bootstrap support but only 58.9% gene-tree and 45.1% site concordance at the deep ingroup node, a pattern consistent with prior evidence that Cx. pallens arose through hybridization between Cx. pipiens and Cx. quinquefasciatus. CAFE5 detected 582 gene families with significant rate departures, and inferred expansions outnumbering contractions on every lineage (counts across all orthogroups with an inferred size change; Cx. quinquefasciatus greatest, 3,733 expanded vs. 729 contracted). Whole-genome ANI ranged 93.1-94.7% (skani); synteny was conserved at the chromosome scale (74-77% collinear anchors) with 258-294 inversions >= 100 kb per pair. Transposable elements occupied a uniform genome fraction (52.7-54.4%). These results refine the divergence framework for the complex, provide evidence consistent with a hybrid origin of Cx. pallens, and establish a pangenomic baseline for future population-level resequencing.

items.title: Hologenomics of xylotrophic bivalves reveals a minimalist, remote-acting evolutionary strategy of wood digestion
items.blurb: Wood constitutes the largest reservoir of biogenic carbon on Earth, yet remarkably few animals can exploit it. While terrestrial wood-feeders like termites rely on highly diverse gut microbiomes, xylotrophic marine bivalves have evolved a fundamentally different approach: a spatially segregated system where intracellular gill symbionts produce enzymes that act remotely within a nearly sterile cecum. However, the genetic and evolutionary basis of this unique symbiosis remains largely elusive. Here, we integrate hologenomics, transcriptomics, and biochemistry of a shallow-water shipworm (Teredo navalis) and a deep-sea borer (Xyloredo sp.). We find that despite diverging approximately 147 million years ago and occupying drastically different habitats, these bivalves maintain a strictly conserved ancestral karyotype and a shared genomic architecture for wood digestion. Our models reveal a clear host-symbiont division of labor. The host genome is specialized for lignin modification and targeted enzyme transport, whereas a highly streamlined symbiont community is responsible for core polysaccharide degradation. Central to this minimalist strategy is a lineage-specific GH5-GH6 dual-catalytic enzyme. By sharing amino acids across proximal binding pockets, this fusion protein unites endo- and exo-cellulase activities, enabling highly synergistic cellulose cleavage without the need for complex microbial communities. Ultimately, our comparative analysis with terrestrial models demonstrates that these marine invertebrates achieve efficient biomass degradation not through microbial expansion, but through extreme functional streamlining and molecular innovation, offering a distinct evolutionary paradigm for marine carbon cycling.

items.title: Patterns and drivers of cranial evolution in rhinos (Rhinocerotoidea; Perissodactyla): allometry, phylogeny and tempo of evolution
items.blurb: Despite their currently scarce taxonomic diversity, rhinocerotoids were among the most evolutionarily successful clades of large herbivorous mammals throughout the Caenozoic. Within an array of morphological adaptations, the cranial horn represents the clades most remarkable and name-giving feature, imposing significant morpho-functional demands on the skull. In this paper, patterns and drivers of the rhinos cranial evolution were investigated for the first time by compiling a three-dimensional geometric morphometric dataset of living and extinct species. Multiple aspects of morphological evolution were explored using phylogenetic comparative methods, including craniofacial evolutionary allometry (CREA - tendency of larger species to have longer faces), phylogenetic constraints, and tempo of evolution. Cranial shape variation linked to horn presence and size evolved under a phylogenetically constrained framework, with a notable transition from hornless to horned species. Rhinos significantly deviated from CREA, likely due to diversity of cranial forms and proportions that evolved independently across the clade in response to varying horn morphologies and dietary habits. Hornless and horned rhinos exhibited similar rates of cranial evolution, and shape variation was obtained through multiple episodes of accelerated evolution. This highlights the role of morphological innovations and Caenozoic global cooling events in the emergence of phenotypic diversity.

items.title: Co-circulating TBEV lineages and evidence for vertical transmission in wild bank voles from Poland
items.blurb: Tick-borne encephalitis virus (TBEV) is a zoonotic flavivirus maintained in complex enzootic cycles involving ticks and vertebrate hosts. While vector-mediated transmission has been extensively studied, host-associated mechanisms, including vertical transmission and prolonged viral carriage in natural reservoir populations, remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated TBEV circulation, genetic diversity, and evidence for vertical transmission in bank voles (Clethrionomys glareolus) from a highly endemic region of North-eastern Poland. A total of 258 wild rodents were screened using molecular and serological approaches. TBEV RNA was detected in 14.3% of individuals, whereas seroprevalence was substantially lower (6.6%), revealing limited concordance between viral presence and humoral response under natural conditions. Near-complete genome sequences were obtained from 10 TBEV-positive individuals, representing the first near-complete TBEV genomes generated from wild rodents in Poland. All isolates belonged to the European subtype (TBEV-Eu), and phylogenetic analysis revealed two genetically distinct viral clades co-circulating within a narrow spatiotemporal window. Importantly, TBEV RNA and/or envelope protein were detected in embryos from naturally infected females, providing evidence consistent with vertical transmission in a wild reservoir host. Together, these findings suggest that vertical transmission and complex host infection dynamics may be underappreciated components of TBEV maintenance in natural reservoir populations. Our results highlight the need to integrate vertebrate host dynamics into models of TBEV ecology and support expanded wildlife-based surveillance to better understand and predict zoonotic risk.

items.title: The IFS Officer Who Raised a Tigress Like His Own Child
items.blurb: What happens when compassion becomes stronger than fear? 🐅❤️ In 1974, a frightened tigress cub was found alone on the banks of Odisha's Khairi River, too young to hunt and too weak to survive. She was brought to Saroj Raj Choudhury, the pioneering forest officer who helped shape Simlipal Tiger Reserve. Knowing she had little chance of surviving alone, he and his wife, Nihar Nalini Swain, brought the cub home, nursed her back to health, and named her Khairi. Khairi didn't grow up as a pet. She grew up as family. She drank milk from their hands, slept beside them, played freely, and formed an extraordinary bond with the couple who had saved her life. When Saroj later tried to return her to the wild, Khairi kept finding her way back home, the only place where she truly felt safe. Over the years, Saroj carefully observed her behaviour, contributing valuable insights to wildlife conservation and our understanding of big cats. In 1981, tragedy struck when Khairi died after contracting rabies following a dog bite. Her loss deeply affected Saroj, who passed away not long afterwards. Until her final days, Nihar continued to call Khairi her daughter. Their story reminds us that conservation isn't only about protecting wildlife, it's also about understanding, respect, and the profound connections that can exist between humans and the natural world. items.title: After Fire Destroyed His Orchard, This Jharkhand Farmer Grew a Rs 40 Lakh Cactus Farm
items.blurb: A hundred litchi trees, 300 mahogany trees, and 900 mango trees – this was the landscape across a 36-acre plot in Bichara village, Jharkhand, back in 2020. The land had been leased by 43-year-old farmer Chaitanya Kumar Ganjhu, who was determined to build something lasting. Every inch of the land was carefully revived to create a thriving orchard. But just three years later, even before the trees had matured, a fire reduced everything to ashes. To this day, Ganjhu does not know who set the blaze. Heartbroken, he could not even claim insurance because no police official was willing to register a complaint. "I didn't have insurance or any supporting document to establish my claim, and I returned home empty-handed," Ganjhu tells The Better India . The ideal species is Opuntia ficus-indica, often referred to as the spineless cactus, which thrives in Indian agroclimatic conditions, particularly in plateau areas such as Jharkhand. His farming journey had begun much earlier. In 2015, he had planned to start a lac farm, but limited resources forced him to change course. Instead, he began planting host trees, including 1,200 Indian jujube trees, only to lose them all in the devastating fire. Spineless cactus showed the way Looking back, Ganjhu now calls the fire a turning point. The tragedy left behind a vast stretch of empty land, forcing him to rethink what he could grow next. While exploring new opportunities in 2024, he learnt about central and state government efforts to promote cactus cultivation. Curious, he reached out to an engineer friend, who suggested that spineless cactus could be worth exploring. "I was excited because cactus farming was completely new to me. During my research, I discovered that natural leather can also be produced using Opuntia ficus-indica , a spineless cactus variety. Our native cactus has thorns, but this one doesn't," he says. Determined to learn more, Ganjhu spent weeks researching online before connecting with the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA). He saw cactus as more than an experimental crop. Unlike lac farming , which generates income only twice a year, cactus offered the possibility of a steadier source of earnings. Encouraged by the government's support for the crop, he contacted ICARDA's centre in Amlaha, Madhya Pradesh, to understand how to begin. Spineless cactus requires very little water, stays green even through harsh summers, and grows well in poor soils. What impressed him most was its resilience. Spineless cactus requires very little water, stays green even through harsh summers, and grows well in poor soils. Because it has no thorns, it can also be used as nutritious fodder for livestock. Confident that the crop had potential, Ganjhu purchased 10,000 cactus cladodes from ICARDA at Rs 10 each. In November 2024, he planted them across 2.5 acres of land at Gamhariya Jaltanda, becoming the first farmer in Jharkhand to cultivate spineless cactus on this scale. Today, his nursery has the capacity to produce nearly two lakh cactus plants every year. He currently grows 25 varieties. Among them, varieties such as Oretha de Elefante Africana, IPA-90-73, Copena V1, Mexica Folder-1278 and Additional-1258, sourced from Brazil, have performed particularly well. Each produces around 10 cladodes annually, compared to two or three from many of the other varieties. The slower-growing varieties, he says, are better suited for research than commercial cultivation. Water for irrigation comes from a solar-powered borewell. During summer, the plants are watered every five to six days because of the poor soil quality. In cooler months, watering once every 15 days is usually enough. Cow dung manure is applied twice a year. According to Dr Shiv Kumar Agrawal, Regional Coordinator for ICARDA's South Asia and China Regional Program and Head of the Food Legume Research Platform, grafting is unnecessary for spineless cactus because of the plant's natural ability to regenerate. "Grafting is not practised at ICARDA because, scientifically, Opuntia already has a high intrinsic regenerative capacity—its cladodes can readily form roots and new shoots without the need for a rootstock. Therefore, grafting does not provide a significant additional advantage in biomass production," explains Dr Agrawal. "Ganjhu is the only farmer to develop a cactus nursery in India. ICARDA introduced this technique and trained district-level officers and officials from the Watershed Development Department, but only Ganjhu took the initiative. Today, he is successfully growing healthy, disease-free spineless cactus in Jharkhand," says Dr Neha Tiwari, National Associate Scientist at ICARDA, Amlaha. Commercial opportunities in cactus farming What began as an experiment soon turned into a business opportunity. "The saplings are essentially cladodes," Ganjhu explains. "When I received an order for 30,000 saplings, I started pruning the mother plants, which made them shorter. I spoke to Dr Neha, who suggested growing them in polybags. From a single cladode, I was able to raise six to eight new saplings and fulfil the entire order." Each sapling takes about four months to grow in a polybag. To meet the demand, Ganjhu employed around 60 women from nearby villages to help prepare and nurture the saplings, creating an additional source of income for them. The economics, he says, are encouraging. A single cladode costs him about Rs 10. From that one cladode, he can grow six saplings, which together sell for around Rs 60. Even after accounting for labour, polybags, soil, irrigation and four months of care, he earns a profit of roughly Rs 25 from a single cladode. His first year was largely about recovering his investment. He spent around Rs 3 lakh procuring planting material and generated almost the same amount through sales. "It has reached the break-even point," he says. "Now the real profits will come." Last year alone, he sold around 30,000 cladodes and saplings at Rs 10 each, including transportation costs. Last year alone, he sold around 30,000 cladodes and saplings at Rs 10 each, including transportation costs. The cactus also serves another purpose on his farm. "I feed it to my goats. During summer, when grass becomes scarce, spineless cactus is a good source of nutrition because it contains high protein," he says. Now, he is waiting for the next big order. Betting on a growing sector Ganjhu believes the timing couldn't be better. The Government of India has identified spineless cactus cultivation as one of the focus areas under the Viksit Bharat framework. In Jharkhand, a project has been planned to cultivate nearly two lakh cactus plants across 400 hectares in different districts. For Ganjhu, this could create a significant opportunity. "If such projects need saplings, where will they source them from?" he asks with a smile. His goal is to become one of the state's key suppliers. Based on the number of cladodes currently available, he estimates he can produce close to four lakh saplings, creating a business worth nearly Rs 40 lakh while generating employment for many rural women. He also plans to participate in future tenders as cactus cultivation expands. Inspiring other farmers Ganjhu's success has already begun influencing neighbouring farmers. Last July, around 15 farmers from Raniyan village, nearly 40 km away in Khunti district, visited his farm after hearing about spineless cactus cultivation. They collected saplings and began planting them on their own land. These farmers are part of the state's cactus promotion initiative, launched in 2025, under which ICARDA has supported growers with free planting material, manure and assistance for land preparation. According to Ganjhu, nearly 40% of the participating farmers have successfully established their plantations. "The department is encouraging farmers to form a cactus growers' association," he says. "Even people who visit my farm often take home 10 or 12 saplings to plant. Slowly, people are beginning to see cactus differently." He enjoys introducing visitors to the wide range of cactus varieties growing on his farm. One of his favourites is Oretha de Elefante Africana, a slender variety that produces fewer cladodes but each weighing nearly half a kilogram. Another, popularly known as the Rabbit Cactus, gets its name from its distinctive pads that resemble rabbit ears. The familiar prickly pear variety also has commercial value. It is used in salads by restaurants and is cooked as a vegetable in several hilly regions. More than an ornamental plant Most people associate cactus with decorative pots or desert landscapes. But spineless cactus has far greater agricultural potential. Broadly, cacti are classified into ornamental, fruit-bearing and fodder varieties. Among these, spineless cactus has emerged as one of the most promising crops because it is easy to handle and serves multiple purposes. Researchers often describe it using the "5F" principle: food, fodder, fuel, fertiliser and fashion. Besides providing nutritious livestock feed, it can contribute to biogas production, organic fertiliser and even bio-leather, opening up new income opportunities for farmers. "The most suitable species is Opuntia ficus-indica , commonly known as nopal or spineless cactus," says Dr Neha Tiwari. "It adapts well to Indian agro-climatic conditions, including plateau regions like Jharkhand. It tolerates drought, fluctuating temperatures and poor soils, making it ideal for rain-fed and degraded lands." Chaitanya Ganjhu cultivates two lakh cactus plants on his 2.5-acre farm. Under field conditions, the plants can grow up to six or seven feet tall, depending on the variety and cultivation practices. Unlike seasonal crops, cactus does not have a fixed maturity period. However, farmers can begin harvesting cladodes around 10 to 12 months after planting, once the plant has established itself with four or five healthy cladodes. A crop built for the future For Ganjhu, spineless cactus is more than a profitable crop. He believes it could help farmers make better use of degraded land while opening up new income streams. "Our native cactus has no commercial value because of its thorns. But spineless cactus can change that," he says. "The soil conditions in Jharkhand are similar to those in parts of Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and West Bengal. If governments continue promoting it, many farmers could benefit." Experts agree. According to Dr Neha Tiwari, National Associate Scientist at ICARDA, Opuntia ficus-indica , commonly known as spineless cactus or nopal, is well suited to Jharkhand's climate because it can tolerate drought, poor soils and fluctuating temperatures. Beyond providing nutritious fodder, the crop has multiple uses. It can be processed into biogas, organic fertiliser and bio-leather, while also contributing to carbon sequestration. Since it requires relatively little water and maintenance once established, researchers see it as a promising option for climate-resilient farming. The initial investment is estimated at Rs 80,000 to Rs 1 lakh per hectare, excluding fencing. However, because the crop remains productive for 15 to 20 years, the long-term maintenance costs are relatively low. For Ganjhu, the bigger challenge is not cultivation but creating a market. "The biggest hurdle is finding buyers," he says. "At present, much of the produce is sent to a processing unit in Uttar Pradesh. If Jharkhand had its own processing unit, it would create jobs and increase farmers' incomes." Demand, however, appears to be growing. ICARDA has been working with the Jharkhand government to promote spineless cactus cultivation by supplying planting material and technical support. As more farmers take up the crop and government-led projects expand, Ganjhu hopes his nursery will become a key source of quality saplings across the state. From ridicule to recognition When Ganjhu first began planting Indian jujube trees years ago, many people in his village laughed at him. "They thought I was wasting my time because those trees already grew everywhere," he recalls. This time, when he introduced spineless cactus, there was scepticism again. But his family stood firmly beside him. Having seen his success in lac farming over the years, they trusted his instincts and encouraged him to continue experimenting. That confidence helped him build a better life. Income from lac farming enabled him to buy first a two-wheeler and later a four-wheeler. He also purchased land to build a house. In 2010, he received an award from the Jharkhand Chief Minister for his contribution to lac production. A farmer who kept looking ahead The fourth of six siblings, Ganjhu grew up in a lower-middle-class farming family. His late father cultivated paddy, oilseeds and vegetables using traditional methods. He attended State Samposhit High School, where three teachers taught nearly 1,000 students. "The teachers would write questions on the blackboard before moving to another classroom because there were so many students," he recalls. After completing school, he earned a BA (Honours) degree from Birsa College in 2003. Finding a job proved difficult. Instead, he discovered an opportunity in lac farming and has specialised in producing high-quality 'Bihan' lac since 2006. Today, he is married and has two sons. When he is not working on the farm, he enjoys travelling and watching cricket. Looking beyond his own farm Despite becoming India's first farmer to establish a commercial spineless cactus nursery, Ganjhu says he is only getting started. His long-term goal is to create a cooperative that can help farmers move beyond cultivation into processing and value addition. "Cactus can be used to produce biogas. The residue becomes fertiliser, and it can also be used to make bio-leather," he says. For him, the dream is no longer just about growing cactus. It is about creating an entire ecosystem around a crop that many once dismissed. After watching thousands of trees disappear in a single fire, Ganjhu could have walked away from farming altogether. Instead, he chose to begin again. Today, the same land that was once reduced to ashes is helping introduce a new crop to Jharkhand — one that could create livelihoods, strengthen climate-resilient farming and inspire more farmers to believe that sometimes, the boldest ideas are the ones worth planting.
